title: To Understand a Century of Conflict in the Middle East, Read This Book
excerpt: Starting with the collapse of the Ottoman Empire after World War I, this book traces how the Middle East's conflicts came about.
body:
Starting with the collapse of the Ottoman Empire after World War I, this book traces how the Middle East's conflicts came about.

## About the Author

Guo Jianlong is a former reporter for *21st Century Business Herald* (《21 世纪经济报道》). He has published a novel, *Farewell, Shangri-La* (《告别香巴拉》), and an "Asia Trilogy" of cultural and historical travel books: *India: The Drifting Subcontinent* (《印度，漂浮的次大陆》), *Under the Mist of the Thousand Pagodas* (《三千佛塔烟云下》) and *Cycling to the Yuan Dynasty* (《骑车去元朝》). He is now traveling the world.

## Excerpt

**Jerusalem: The Exiles Come Home**

Even today, at the southernmost tip of Egypt, you can find traces of Jews who lived there more than 2,000 years ago. In Aswan, a city in Egypt's south, the most pleasant thing a visitor can do is board a felucca (a small three-masted sailboat) and drift back in time. Within Egypt the Nile is a river without tributaries. Look out from the water and you see vast dunes and stony desert on both banks; only along the river's edge do two thin strips of green run, and here and there, where the river bends, the green widens to a few kilometers or a dozen or so, enough for crops and date palms. These green places have been Egypt's lifeline from ancient times to now. Only on the Nile do the secrets of Egypt's 5,000 years lie open to view. A felucca has no engine; it moves only by wind and current. When the wind blows, the boatman struggles with the sail and the rudder at the stern; when it drops, the boat simply drifts.

Since the time of the pharaohs, boats like these have carried stone, obelisks, building materials and grain. Going downstream from Aswan to the Nile Delta near Cairo takes roughly ten-odd days to a month; the return, against the current, takes longer still.

In Cleopatra's day, the Egyptian queen and her lovers rode such boats from Alexandria to Cairo, feasting and carousing the whole way, enjoying the best of times.

This way of life lasted into the 19th century. Napoleon's invasion of Egypt failed, but the ruler who came after, Muhammad Ali Pasha, was a Westernizer, and Egypt gradually entered the itinerary of Europe's Grand Tour. The European traveler's dream was to rent a small boat and sail up the Nile, past the pyramids of Giza, Memphis (capital of the Old Kingdom), Asyut, Abydos, Luxor (capital of the New Kingdom), Esna, Edfu, Kom Ombo and Aswan, all the way to Abu Simbel on the border with Sudan. By day they rested in the shade of mango trees on the bank and smoked a little hashish or a water pipe; at dawn and dusk they sailed on; at night they slept on board or found lodging in a riverside village.

Steamboats slowly broke this leisurely pace, but traces of the past remain. On the stretch of the Nile between Aswan and Luxor, feluccas are everywhere. Walk into a café, find a captain puffing on his water pipe, rent his boat, and you are instantly back 100, 1,000 or 3,000 years.

In Aswan I rented a small boat from a Nubian captain. The Nubians are an ancient people of Egypt, present since the time of the pharaohs. They are darker than most Egyptians and handsomer of face; even without make-up, they look as if they have stepped out of antiquity. Upper Egypt, where Aswan lies, is one of the Nubian heartlands.

My plan was to take the boat downriver the next day, swim in the Nile, eat on board and rest under the trees outside a small Nubian village. So that I could judge the boat, the captain took me out the day before for a trial run around Elephantine Island.

Elephantine is an island in the Nile ringed by smooth boulders shaped like elephants drinking at the water's edge, hence its name. It was once a central city of ancient Egypt and a stronghold of Upper Egypt. In the pharaohs' time, the site of today's Aswan was still wasteland, while Elephantine already thrived. Soldiers sent from the north to guard the frontier and merchants coming up from the south met here, and a busy market grew.

From the boat, the captain pointed out the ruins of the ancient city and the nilometer, a gauge for measuring the river's level. The Nile rises and falls dramatically each year; the volume of water in the flood season can be ten times that of the dry season. When the river floods, it covers the land along its banks; when the water recedes, the land it soaked is left rich with organic matter carried from East Africa and the Ethiopian Highlands, and exceptionally fertile. A Nile flood meant a good harvest the following year, and people could forecast the coming crop from the level marked on the nilometer.

As the captain went through the sights one by one, he suddenly said: "You may not know this, but this was also the southernmost Jewish settlement in Egypt. It's been here 3,000 years..."

According to written records dug up on Elephantine, a community of Jewish traders lived here around the 6th century BC. In that century the Jews of Jerusalem suffered one of the darkest events in their history: the Babylonians destroyed the First Temple they had built, and carried many Jews off to Babylon as exiles. This was the moment the Jewish Diaspora across the world began.

Egypt and the Jews share deep roots. Some modern scholars believe that the main line of monotheism, represented by Judaism, Christianity and Islam, may trace back to the pharaoh Akhenaten. Because the priesthood had grown too powerful, Akhenaten launched a sweeping religious reform. He abolished Egypt's many gods and worshipped only one, the sun god Aten.

After Akhenaten died his reform was undone, but his monotheism influenced the Jews then living in Egypt. When Moses led the Jews out of Egypt, monotheism went with them to the Middle East and eventually became Judaism. Christianity and Islam later carried the monotheistic tradition down to the present day.

Even after Moses led the Jews out of Egypt, the bond between Egypt and the Jews did not vanish. In 586 BC, Nebuchadnezzar II, king of the Neo-Babylonian Empire, conquered the Jewish kingdom, razed the famous Temple of Solomon and deported part of the Jewish population to Babylon (in present-day Iraq). This was the famous Babylonian captivity. Besides those in Babylon and Jerusalem, some Jews, under persecution, fled their homes for the Nile Delta in Egypt (near where Alexandria would later rise), which also became a Jewish settlement. From there they spread on to North Africa and across Upper Egypt.

Alexandria today is one of Egypt's liveliest cities. It sits on the Mediterranean, is easy to reach and is a crossroads for people on the move. In Alexandria, to my surprise, I met several refugees from Syria. They told me they had fled the war and were on their way to Libya. I was astonished, because Libya too is at war, and its eastern region near Egypt in particular has been infiltrated by too many extremist religious groups; it is not safe. But they said they were going to Libya because from there it was easy to get to Europe. Going straight from Syria into Europe was all but impossible, while if they went the long way round through Libya, the Europeans rarely asked questions. So to reach Europe, a moment's risk was worth taking.

I sighed: how much the present resembles 2,000 years ago! The same refugees, the same flight, the same route, the same blood, tears and suffering; the only difference is the religion.

With Alexandria as their center, the ancient Jews spread to every corner of Egypt, including that small island at its southern end. The Jewish community found on Elephantine shows how vigorous this trading people was: they had traveled from distant Jerusalem to Aswan, at the end of the known world.

Later, Persia conquered Babylon, and the Jews were allowed to go home. Some went back; some did not. Those who stayed became the earliest pioneers of the Jewish settlement of the Middle East beyond Jerusalem.

But the Jews' good days in Jerusalem lasted only a few hundred years before they entered 2,000 years of exile. In the Roman period, Pompey conquered Jerusalem and placed it under Roman protection. But the Jews would not submit to Roman rule; they rose up several times and were crushed several times. In AD 70 the Second Temple (the Temple of Solomon was the First) was destroyed, and in AD 135 the Emperor Hadrian razed Jerusalem and barred Jews from living there. The Jews were driven from their homes once more, and this time the exile lasted 2,000 years.

The Jews who left Jerusalem scattered across the world and gradually split into several branches. The best known are the Ashkenazi Jews, who lived mainly in Eastern and Northern Europe. Because most of them lived in German-controlled territory during World War II, they suffered catastrophic losses. In Poland, 3 million Jews died, more than 90% of the total; in Ukraine, 60% of Jews died; add the Soviet-controlled areas and the areas under direct German rule, and countless people were reduced to heaps of bones.

Yet what happened to the Ashkenazim had already happened to other branches long before. In 1492, Spain persecuted another branch of the Jews.

After the Ashkenazim, the second-largest branch is the Sephardic Jews, also called the Western branch, who lived mainly on the Iberian Peninsula, home to Spain and Portugal, and in North Africa, France, Turkey, the Middle East and elsewhere. That they were scattered so widely was itself the result of persecution. In 1492, the same year Columbus reached the New World, the Spanish king led a campaign much like Hitler's persecution of the Jews. Every Jew in his kingdom had a few choices: convert to Christianity; leave their property behind and quit the king's lands with a small bundle; or be killed.

At the time, the vast majority of the world's Jews were Sephardim. But as the persecution went on, they died, fled or converted, and many who fled north became Ashkenazim. Sephardim had once made up 97% of all Jews; by the eve of World War II, Ashkenazim made up 92%. Persecution was the cause of the Sephardim's decline.

While Spain persecuted the Sephardim, Islam held out a hand of friendship. The Ottoman Empire was then at its height and badly needed skilled craftsmen and capital, so the Ottoman sultan invited Jews to settle in his lands. On Ottoman soil, the Jews flourished at once.

Jewish communities prospered across the empire: in its European territories (Istanbul above all), in Bursa in Asia, and in its other Middle Eastern holdings (Iraq, Syria, Egypt). The Middle East became once again one of the main places where Jews lived.

While studying the history of Eurasia, I also came across a people called the Khazars. This people, who lived in the 8th century north of the Caucasus Mountains, between the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea, were, of all things, tied to Judaism.

At that time China was under the Tang dynasty and Europe was in the Middle Ages, while the Russians still lived in darkness and had yet to form a state. The mighty Turkic empire had just collapsed, and Islam was midway between its rise and its golden age. Just then, a strange state that professed Judaism appeared at the very center of Eurasia: the Khazar Khaganate.

The Khazars were a nomadic Turkic people. Their state appeared 600 years after the Jews lost Jerusalem and more than a thousand years before the founding of modern Israel, which made it the only state in those 2,000 years to profess Judaism.

The Khazars took up Judaism as a strategy for survival. Their era coincided with fierce rivalry between Islam to the east and Christianity to the west. To the Khazars' southeast lay the powerful Caliphate; to their southwest, the Eastern Roman Empire of Constantinople (today's Istanbul). Each side wanted to win the Khazars over to its own faith. Sitting astride the trade routes between Asia and Europe, the Khazar state needed to trade with both and could afford to offend neither, so the Khazar khagan hit upon a clever solution: convert to Judaism.

Both Christianity and Islam acknowledge in their own histories that Judaism is a source of their faith. The Old Testament comes directly from Jewish records. Islam recognizes the Jewish prophets, such as King David and Moses.

By choosing Judaism, the khagan hoped to keep both sides on good terms, but without meaning to, he made his country the only one in 2,000 years to profess Judaism. Some have even traced the origins of the Ashkenazim to the Khazars, arguing that the Ashkenazim entered Eastern Europe with Khazar help, or even that they carry Khazar blood.

Genetic studies, however, have found no direct link between the Ashkenazi bloodline and the peoples of the Caucasus, which settles this long-running mystery. Still, the Khazar case shows how widely Jews and Judaism had spread.

Jews are also said to have been active in China during the Tang and Song dynasties, especially in Kaifeng, the Song capital.

Of course, every move into a wider world came with untold blood and tears, and only by understanding what the Jews suffered over those 2,000 years can one see why they longed so much to go home. In the late 19th century, anti-Jewish feeling spread across Europe again, from Tsarist Russia to France. Tsarist Russia's persecution of the Jews had long been an open secret, and the policy even carried over into the Red, Soviet era after the tsars fell. In France, the Dreyfus Affair deepened Jewish fears that before long all of Europe might become their grave. It was then that a new movement, one unseen in 2,000 years, arose among the Jews: Zionism.

This time, instead of simply fleeing as before, the Jews began to ask why their people had been persecuted and forced to run for 2,000 years. Their answer: because the Jews had no homeland of their own. To end a life of wandering and hardship, they needed a base. And so Mount Zion, the ancient hill in Jerusalem, became the Zionists' symbol.

But why did the Jews' base have to be in Jerusalem?

The British once tried to persuade the Jews to accept a tract of land somewhere in British Africa, but were turned down. The Zionists understood clearly that only their old homeland, Jerusalem, could truly capture the attention of Jews around the world.

Better still for them, Jerusalem happened to be under the control of a moribund empire, one that had always been friendly to the Jews and had helped them before.

So fundraising organizations were founded, and banks were set up to lend to immigrants. Jews who had gone to the New World of America, being clever, had mostly grown rich, and they gave large sums to support the movement. Jews in Eastern Europe, being poor, were also willing to try their luck somewhere else.

Had the movement stayed within the Ottoman political system, with Jews and Arabs in Jerusalem alike obeying Ottoman law, equal in politics and rivals in business, and with the Ottoman government stepping in as a neutral arbiter whenever conflict broke out, Jewish immigration would have been peaceful. But the two world wars upset the balance of the region.

After World War I, the Ottoman Empire was gone, and Palestine became a British mandate. Jews and Arabs both suddenly realized that once the British mandate ended, they might form independent states and exercise full sovereignty. Both also realized that whichever side formed a state first would inevitably rule over the other, and that whether Jews ruled Arabs or Arabs ruled Jews, neither would stay neutral as the Ottoman Empire had; either way, one people would be oppressing another.

After World War II, as the whole world reeled from Hitler's Holocaust, the Zionists finally seized their chance. In 1947 the United Nations announced that two states would be created in Palestine, and in 1948 the British withdrew. The Jews at last fulfilled a 2,000-year-old dream: the wanderers had come home.
